examples.input: Run a command while the watcher is running in the same project

results.1: The command waits until the watcher finishes its current step, then runs. Nothing new appears in `.troupe/`.
results.2: The command waits until the watcher finishes its current step, then runs. A lock file appears in `.troupe/` and stays there.

examples.input: A command is killed partway through (Ctrl-C, crash, `kill -9`)

results.1: The next command runs right away. The system drops the lock when the process dies, and there's nothing left to clean up.
results.2: The next command runs right away. The system drops the lock when the process dies. The lock file stays behind, but it's harmless and doesn't need deleting.

examples.input: Run a command in a project whose `.troupe/` folder you can read but not write

results.1: The lock is taken on the folder itself, so no new file has to be created and the command doesn't need write access just to lock.
results.2: If the lock file can't be created, it falls back to opening it read-only, so locking can still work if the file already exists.

context.in_practice: Both routes make commands and the watcher take turns, and neither leaves a stale lock that blocks people after a crash. Users see the difference mainly as one extra file in `.troupe/` under route 2. Maintainers see it elsewhere. Route 1 relies on locking a folder, which is less common, and some systems or network drives may not support it. Route 2 is the usual approach and is easy to recognise, but it adds a file that tools copying or cleaning the store have to cope with. Under both routes, a second command waits with no time limit rather than failing.
context.stakes: When two commands, or a command and the watcher, touch the project's `.troupe` store at the same time, one has to wait so they don't corrupt each other's changes. What differs is whether the store gets an extra file, and how locking behaves when the folder can't be written to.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 adds no file to the store but depends on locking a folder, which is less usual. Route 2 uses the familiar lock-file approach but leaves a permanent extra file in `.troupe/` and needs a read-only fallback.

plan_why: Both routes are locks that only matter when two troupe processes run at once. The sandbox runs commands one after another and forbids `watch`, so they never compete for the lock, and every command gives the same output, exit code and file contents under either route. The only visible difference is that route 2 leaves a lock file under .troupe/. The contract allows that, and its name is up to each implementation, so no fixed `show` list could reliably reveal it.
